stem: Transection of the anterolateral tract of the spinal cord results in which of the following clinical features:
options: Loss of pain and temperature sensation
Loss of vibration and fine-touch sensation
fact: The anterolateral/spinothalamic system carries pain and temperature; interruption produces a contralateral deficit beginning below the lesion.
finding: The spinothalamic tract reference supports pain and temperature loss after anterolateral tract injury.

stem: A 65 year old lady presents to ED complaining of sudden onset visual loss. On examination you demonstrate visual loss on the right side of the vertical midline with macular sparing in both eyes. Which of the following blood vessels is most likely occluded:
fact: The posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital visual cortex; infarction can cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.
finding: The posterior-circulation reference supports PCA supply to the occipital visual cortex.

stem: A 65 year old lady, with a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus, presents to ED with a 1 hour history of sudden onset of weakness and numbness solely in her left leg and foot. She is placed on the stroke pathway. Which of the following blood vessels has most likely been occluded:
fact: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial frontal and parietal cortex, including the paracentral lobule for contralateral lower-limb motor and sensory function.
finding: The anterior cerebral artery reference supports medial hemisphere and lower-limb cortical supply.

stem: You are performing a full neurological examination on a patient who has presented to the ED department with generalised weakness. You note she has a unilateral absence of her triceps reflex. Which spinal nerve is primarily responsible for this reflex:
fact: The triceps tendon reflex primarily tests the C7 spinal cord segment and nerve root.
mnemonic: C7 extends the elbow and drives the triceps reflex.
finding: The deep-tendon-reflex reference supports C7 as the principal triceps reflex segment.

stem: The primary visual cortex is located in which of the following regions:
fact: The primary visual cortex is located in the occipital lobe around the calcarine sulcus.
finding: The visual-pathway reference supports occipital localization of primary visual cortex.

stem: What type of visual field defect are you likely to see in a lesion of the visual cortex:
options: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
fact: A visual-cortex lesion causes contralateral homonymous hemianopia; macular sparing may occur because the occipital pole has dual vascular supply.
mnemonic: Cortex cuts the opposite half but often spares the macula.
finding: The visual-field reference supports contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing from visual-cortex lesions.

stem: A patient complains of diplopia on reading or walking downstairs, which of the following cranial nerves is most likely to be affected:
options: Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve
fact: Trochlear nerve palsy weakens the superior oblique, causing impaired downward gaze and vertical diplopia, often noticed when reading or walking downstairs.
mnemonic: SO4: superior oblique is cranial nerve IV.
finding: The trochlear-nerve reference supports the displayed clinical pattern.

stem: A 64 year old lady complains of a sore right eye. On examination, you note a normal corneal blink reflex on her left side but no consensual blink reflex on her right side. A lesion in which of the following structures is most likely to cause this clinical picture:
fact: The corneal reflex is afferent through the ophthalmic division of CN V and efferent through CN VII; loss of the right efferent limb causes absent right consensual blink.
mnemonic: V1 feels the cornea; VII closes the eye.
finding: The facial-nerve reference supports CN VII as the efferent corneal-reflex pathway.

stem: Oculomotor (CN III) palsy with sparing of the pupillary reflex is most likely caused by which of the following:
options: Aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery
fact: Diabetic ischemic CN III palsy typically affects central motor fibres and may spare the peripheral parasympathetic pupillary fibres; compressive lesions more often dilate the pupil.
mnemonic: Diabetes keeps the pupil alive; compression opens it.
finding: The oculomotor-nerve reference supports pupil-sparing diabetic ischemic palsy.

stem: Which of the following clinical features would you most expect to see in a glossopharyngeal nerve palsy:
fact: CN IX is the afferent limb of the gag reflex, so glossopharyngeal palsy can cause loss of the gag reflex; uvular deviation and hoarseness are more associated with CN X.
mnemonic: IX initiates the gag; X executes the voice and palate.
finding: The glossopharyngeal-nerve reference supports loss of gag reflex as the expected finding.
